decks.title: How to Tell Wild Animals — Carolyn Wells
goals: Explain the central idea of the poem stanza by stanza, in your own words
Explain the humorous ways of identifying each animal
Identify humour, rhyme, irony and deliberate misspelling and say what they do
Describe the poem's form and its punchline couplets
Answer extract-based and 40–50 word questions on the poem

slides.heading: How to Tell Wild Animals — Carolyn Wells
slides.body_md:
*First Flight*, poetry · Class 10 CBSE English.

slides.narration: Welcome. Today’s poem is How to Tell Wild Animals by Carolyn Wells, the funniest poem in your book. Please read it in First Flight now, aloud, twice, and enjoy it. We will not repeat its lines here. Instead we will see how the joke works in every stanza, what each animal’s test is, and how to answer board questions on the poem.

slides.heading: How to read a humorous poem
bullets: Read it aloud twice from *First Flight*, with a straight face.
For each stanza ask: which animal? what is the test? why is it funny?
Notice the last two lines of every stanza: that is where the joke lands.
In answers, explain in your own words; never copy lines.
slides.narration: Humorous poems are best read aloud, with a straight face, like a serious lecture. For each stanza ask three questions: which animal is it, what is the test, and why is it funny? Watch the last two lines of every stanza, because that is where the joke lands. In the exam, explain in your own words. Copying lines does not earn marks.

slides.heading: The poet: Carolyn Wells

rows: humorous and nonsense verse, parodies and riddles
edited collections of comic poetry; wrote many mystery novels

visual.alt: Table of facts about Carolyn Wells: an American writer, 1862 to 1942, known for humorous and nonsense verse, who edited collections of comic poetry and wrote many mystery novels.

slides.narration: Carolyn Wells was an American writer who lived from eighteen sixty-two to nineteen forty-two. She loved comic and nonsense verse, wrote parodies and riddles, and edited collections of funny poems. She also wrote many mystery novels. This poem shows her favourite trick: saying something silly in a perfectly serious voice.

slides.heading: The poem at a glance

rows: ababcc in every stanza: the couplet is the punchline
a mock expert advising "you", the reader
one animal per stanza (stanza 5 has two)
grand words, old-fashioned contractions, playful spellings

visual.alt: Table of the poem at a glance: six stanzas of six lines rhyming a b a b c c, a mock expert advising the reader, one animal per stanza with two in stanza five, grand words and playful spellings, and a light-hearted, mock-serious, ironic tone.

slides.narration: Here is the poem at a glance. Six stanzas of six lines, each rhyming a b a b c c, so every stanza ends with a rhyming couplet that delivers the punchline. The speaker is a mock expert advising you, the reader. There is one animal in each stanza, except the fifth, which has two. And the tone is light-hearted and mock-serious.

slides.heading: The joke behind every stanza
slides.body_md: The title promises a practical guide. But almost every test identifies the animal only when it is already attacking you, so the knowledge arrives too late to help. That is situational irony, delivered in a calm, teacherly voice.
slides.narration: Before we meet the animals, notice the single joke behind the poem. The title promises a useful guide. But almost every test tells you which animal it is only when it is already attacking you. By then the knowledge is useless. That is situational irony, and the calm, polite voice of the speaker makes it even funnier.

slides.heading: Stanzas 1 and 2: the lion and the tiger
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: wandering in eastern forests, if a huge yellowish-brown animal roars over you as you lie dying, you have met the Asiatic lion. If a handsome striped animal welcomes you on a walk, observe whether it makes a meal of you; that will settle that you have met the tiger.
slides.narration: The first two stanzas deal with the big cats of Asia. In eastern forests, if a huge yellowish-brown animal roars over you as you lie dying, you may conclude you have met the Asiatic lion. And if a handsome striped animal welcomes you on your walk, simply observe whether it makes a meal of you. That will tell you that you have met the tiger.

slides.heading: Stanzas 3 and 4: the leopard and the bear
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: an animal with a spotted coat that springs on you must be the leopard, and crying out is useless, since it will keep springing. An animal met close to home that crushes you in a hug is the bear. Should you still doubt, it will hug you again, and the poet calls this a caress.
slides.narration: Next, the leopard. If an animal with a spotted coat springs on you, you have met the leopard, and there is no point crying out, because it will only keep springing. Then the bear, met close to home. Its crushing hug identifies it, and if you are still unsure, it will hug you again. The poet calls that deadly squeeze a caress.

slides.heading: Check: the bear
slides.narration: Your turn. How, according to the poem, can you be certain that you have met a bear? Choose the answer that matches the poet’s test.

slides.heading: Stanzas 5 and 6: the crocodile, the hyena and the chameleon
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: a beginner may be puzzled by hunting animals, but there is a rule: the one that comes grinning is the hyena; the one that weeps is the crocodile. Last, the chameleon: a small lizard with no ears and no wings. If you look at a branch and see nothing, you are looking at a chameleon.
slides.narration: The fifth stanza admits that beginners may be puzzled, then offers a rule. The animal that comes grinning is the hyena; the one that weeps is the crocodile. The last stanza changes the pattern. The chameleon, by contrast, stays tiny and harmless, a little lizard with no ears and no wings. If you look at a branch and see nothing at all, you have found a chameleon.

visual.alt: Table of the animals stanza by stanza: the Asiatic lion, known when it roars over you as you lie dying; the tiger, by whether it makes a meal of you; the leopard, by springing on you; the bear, by its hug; the hyena by its grin and the crocodile by its tears; and the chameleon, by finding the branch apparently empty.

slides.narration: Here is every stanza in one table. Notice the real feature behind each joke: the lion’s coat and roar, the tiger’s stripes, the leopard’s spots and leap, the bear’s strength, the hyena’s laugh-like call, the idiom crocodile tears, and the chameleon’s camouflage. The poet starts from facts and pushes each one into absurdity.

slides.heading: The pattern of a stanza

visual.alt: Flow of a typical stanza: an animal appears, its looks or behaviour are described, the absurd test is given, and the punchline arrives in the closing couplet.
visual.caption: The pattern of a typical stanza (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Almost every stanza follows the same pattern. An animal appears. Its looks or behaviour are described. Then comes the absurd test. And the rhyming couplet at the end delivers the punchline. Once you spot this pattern, you can explain any stanza in an exam, and you can even write a funny stanza of your own.

slides.heading: Check: assertion and reason
slides.narration: Check yourself with an assertion and reason. Both statements may be true, but does the second really explain the first? Think about what the crocodile’s tears are based on.

slides.heading: Themes and message
bullets: **Humour and wordplay:** the poem's main aim is delight.
**Parody:** it mocks guides that promise more than they deliver.
**A quiet reminder:** wild animals are powerful; close encounters can be fatal.
**Language as fun:** rhyme, spelling and idiom are played with.
slides.narration: What is the poem about? Mainly delight: it wants us to laugh. The poem is also a parody, mocking guides that promise more than they deliver. Underneath, there is a quiet reminder that wild animals are powerful, and that meeting one up close can be fatal. And it celebrates language as play. In answers, say that its purpose is to entertain.

visual.alt: Table of poetic devices in the poem, described, each with a SOYL example: situational irony, verbal irony, poetic licence, an idiom taken literally, a mock-serious tone and the a b a b c c rhyme.

slides.narration: Now the devices. Situational irony: each animal is known only when it attacks. Verbal irony: a deadly hug called a caress. Poetic licence: words clipped or respelt for rhyme and fun. An idiom taken literally: crocodile tears. A mock-serious tone. And the a b a b c c rhyme. The examples on the right are our own sentences.

slides.heading: Worked point: deliberate misspellings
slides.body_md: Find two unusual spellings in *First Flight*: one in the lion stanza and one in the leopard stanza. They are not mistakes.
bullets: **Lion stanza:** a word for dying is clipped with an apostrophe so that it rhymes with the animal's name.
**Leopard stanza:** the verb for jumping is respelt so that it echoes the first syllable of the animal's name.
**Term:** poetic licence, a poet's freedom to bend the rules for rhyme, rhythm or effect.
**Effect:** the rhyme stays neat and the playful spelling adds to the comedy.
slides.narration: Here is a worked point. In the lion stanza, a word for dying is clipped with an apostrophe so that it rhymes with the animal’s name. In the leopard stanza, the verb for jumping is respelt to echo the first syllable of the animal’s name. These are not mistakes. They are poetic licence, used for rhyme, rhythm and fun.

slides.heading: Tone
slides.body_md: Light-hearted and mock-serious. The speaker sounds like a polite expert giving sensible advice, with grand words and old-fashioned contractions, while the advice itself is absurd and comes too late.
slides.narration: Listen to the tone. The speaker sounds like a polite expert, calm and confident, using grand words like discern and nonplus and old-fashioned contractions. But the advice is absurd and arrives too late. This gap between a serious manner and a silly message is called a mock-serious tone, and that gap drives the poem’s comedy.

slides.heading: Word meanings

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: tawny, discern, peppered, caress, novice and nonplus.
visual.caption: Single words from the poem with their meanings.

slides.narration: A few words to know. Tawny, yellowish-brown. Discern, to make out or recognise. Peppered, sprinkled all over. Caress, a gentle, loving touch. Novice, a beginner. And nonplus, to puzzle or confuse. Several of these grand words add to the mock-serious tone, so mention that when you explain them.

slides.heading: Check: the rhyme scheme
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the rhyme scheme of one stanza using letters. Look in your textbook at which line endings share a sound, and notice the last two lines.

slides.heading: Worked example: a 40–50 word answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* How does the poet make the bear stanza funny?
bullets: **Point:** a deadly encounter is described as if it were affectionate.
**Animal and test (own words):** the bear, met close to home, is known by its crushing hug.
**Why funny:** if you still doubt, it hugs again; the squeeze is called a caress.

**Model (46 words):** *The poet turns a deadly meeting into a joke. A bear met close to home is known by its crushing hug, and if you still have doubts, it will hug you again. Calling this killing squeeze a caress, a tender touch, is irony that makes us laugh.*

slides.narration: Here is how to build a three mark answer. Find the key word: funny. State the point: a deadly meeting is treated as affectionate. Give the animal and its test in your own words. Then say why it is funny: the second hug, and the ironic word caress. The model is forty-six words and quotes nothing.

slides.heading: Check: the idiom
slides.narration: One more. Which well-known idiom does the crocodile and hyena stanza take literally? Think about how the crocodile is identified.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A mock guide: almost every animal is identified only when it attacks.
Lion, tiger, leopard, bear, crocodile and hyena, chameleon: each with an absurd test.
Form: 6 stanzas of 6 lines, ababcc; the couplet is the punchline.
Devices: situational and verbal irony, poetic licence, idiom taken literally, mock-serious tone.
Purpose: to entertain, with a quiet reminder that wild animals are dangerous. Read the poem in *First Flight*.

visual.alt: Flow of a typical stanza: an animal appears, its looks or behaviour are described, the absurd test is given, and the punchline arrives in the closing couplet.
visual.caption: The pattern of a typical stanza (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Let us sum up. The poem is a mock guide in which almost every animal is identified only when it attacks. Six stanzas of six lines, rhyming a b a b c c, with a punchline couplet. Irony, poetic licence, an idiom taken literally and a mock-serious tone make it funny. Its purpose is to entertain, with a quiet reminder about real danger.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write out the poem's lines; describe each animal's test in your own words.
Explain why each test is funny: it comes too late, or it rests on a paradox.
Name devices **and** say what they do: *calling the hug a caress is irony*.
40–50 word answers: point + animal and test + why it is funny.
Common slips: calling the spellings mistakes; saying the chameleon attacks; mixing up hyena and crocodile.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never write out the lines; describe each test in your own words. Always explain why it is funny. When you name a device, say what it does. Keep three mark answers to point, test and humour. And avoid the common slips: the spellings are deliberate, the chameleon does no harm, and the hyena is the one that grins while the crocodile weeps.

sections.heading: 1. The poet and the poem
sections.body_md:
**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

**Carolyn Wells** (1862–1942) was an American writer of humorous and nonsense verse, parodies and riddles. She edited collections of comic poetry and also wrote many mystery novels. *How to Tell Wild Animals* pretends to be a practical guide to recognising dangerous animals.

sections.heading: 2. What happens (SOYL summary)
sections.body_md:
**Stanza 1 — the Asiatic lion:** the huge yellowish-brown animal that roars over you in an eastern forest as you lie dying.

**Stanza 2 — the tiger:** the handsome striped animal that welcomes you; observe whether it makes a meal of you.

**Stanza 3 — the leopard:** the spotted animal that springs on you; crying out is useless, since it keeps springing.

**Stanza 4 — the bear:** met close to home, known by its crushing hug, which it repeats if you doubt; the poet calls it a caress.

**Stanza 5 — the hyena and the crocodile:** a rule for beginners: the grinning one is the hyena, the weeping one the crocodile.

**Stanza 6 — the chameleon:** a small lizard without ears or wings; if a branch looks empty, you have found a chameleon.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Humour:** the main purpose is to entertain.
- **Parody:** the poem mocks guidebooks that promise expert knowledge but are useless in a real emergency.
- **A quiet reminder:** wild animals are powerful, and close encounters can be fatal.
- **Delight in language:** rhyme, playful spellings and idioms taken literally.

sections.heading: 4. Devices, humour and form
sections.body_md:
**Situational irony:** the tests identify each animal (apart from the harmless chameleon) only when it attacks.

**Verbal irony:** the bear's deadly hug is called a caress.

**Poetic licence (deliberate misspelling):** in the lion stanza a word for dying is clipped to rhyme with the animal's name; in the leopard stanza the verb for jumping is respelt to echo the first syllable of the animal's name. Old-fashioned contractions and inverted word order also fit the rhyme.

**Idiom taken literally:** crocodile tears (false sorrow) becomes the crocodile's identifying mark; the hyena's laugh-like call explains its grin.

**Form:** six stanzas of six lines; rhyme scheme ababcc; the closing couplet delivers the punchline.

key_terms.definition_md: A poet's freedom to bend spelling, grammar or word order for rhyme, rhythm or effect.
When what happens is the opposite of what was expected (a guide that helps only when it is too late).
Treating a silly subject in a solemn, learned manner for comic effect.

sections.heading: 7. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints the poem's lines; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Expect questions on each animal's test, the misspellings, irony, the idiom and the rhyme scheme.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + animal and test in your own words + why it is funny.

Practise with the poem itself in *First Flight*; never reproduce its lines in an answer.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5) and short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) on First Flight poems (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** a correct point, support from the poem in your own words, and accurate expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing out the poem instead of explaining it.
2. Calling the unusual spellings mistakes instead of poetic licence.
3. Mixing up the hyena (grins) and the crocodile (weeps).
4. Saying the chameleon attacks.
5. Describing the tests without explaining why they are funny.

**Remember:** read the poem in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.passage_md: Carolyn Wells dresses her poem up as a practical guide. Its title promises useful advice, and each stanza seems to teach the reader how to recognise one more dangerous animal. But the advice is a trap. Again and again, the sure sign that you have met a particular animal is that it is already attacking you. By the time you can name it, you are in no position to use the knowledge. The joke works because the poem keeps a straight face, offering absurd tests in the calm voice of a schoolteacher.

If, wandering through eastern forests, you are approached by a huge animal with a yellowish-brown coat that roars over you as you lie dying, you may conclude that you have met the Asiatic lion. questions.passage_md: The leopard and the bear stanzas push the joke further. The leopard is recognised by its spotted coat, but only once it has sprung on you; crying out will be useless, because it will simply keep springing. Here the poet bends the spelling of the verb so that it echoes the first syllable of the animal's name, a bit of play that adds to the comedy. The bear, met unexpectedly close to home, is recognised by its crushing embrace. If you are still unsure, it will hug you again, and the poet calls that deadly squeeze a caress.

questions.passage_md: Is there anything serious under the fun? Perhaps a little. The poem mocks guidebooks that promise more than they deliver, and it gently reminds us that wild animals are not toys or curiosities: they are powerful, and close encounters can be fatal. But Wells does not preach. Her real gift to the reader is delight in language: in rhyme that snaps shut at the end of each stanza, in playful spellings, in idioms taken literally. This poem is meant to be read aloud, enjoyed and remembered, perhaps the first poem in the book that students laugh at.

answer.model_answer_md: How to Tell Wild Animals is funny in several ways. If you are relaxing on your terrace with a plate of pakoras and a grey shape snatches one from your hand before vanishing over the wall, you have met the monkey. answer.model_answer_md:
Laugh at the Poem, Respect the Animal

Carolyn Wells's How to Tell Wild Animals makes us laugh because every animal is identified only once it attacks. In real life, that is no laughing matter. Whether we visit a national park or come across a monkey in our colony, a few rules keep both people and animals safe. Watch from a distance and never feed wild animals. Follow the instructions of forest guides. Keep food covered and avoid sudden movements. Remember that animals attack mostly when they feel threatened or cornered. Above all, respect their space: we are visitors in their home. Enjoy the poem, but leave the identification tests to the page.

answer.model_answer_md: Poetic licence is the freedom a poet takes to break the ordinary rules of language, spelling or grammar for the sake of rhyme, rhythm or effect. Carolyn Wells uses it playfully. In the lion stanza, a word for dying is clipped with an apostrophe so that it rhymes with the animal's name. In the leopard stanza, the verb for jumping is respelt in two forms that echo the first syllable of the animal's name, a sly pun. She also uses old-fashioned contractions and inverted word order, as in poetry of earlier times, to fit her rhyme scheme. These liberties are never careless; they are part of the comedy and make the poem bouncy and memorable.

questions.stem_md: *How to Tell Wild Animals* was written by the American writer Carolyn ___.
questions.solution_md: The poet is Carolyn **Wells**.

questions.stem_md: A poet's freedom to bend spelling or grammar for rhyme or effect, as in *How to Tell Wild Animals*, is called poetic ___.
questions.solution_md: It is poetic **licence**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In *How to Tell Wild Animals*, the animal that weeps is said to be the crocodile.

**Reason (R):** The hyena in *How to Tell Wild Animals* is said to come grinning.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A rests on the idiom crocodile tears, not on how the hyena behaves.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The identification tests in *How to Tell Wild Animals* are of no practical use.

**Reason (R):** In *How to Tell Wild Animals*, most animals can be recognised only once they are attacking.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the timing of the tests is exactly why they are useless.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Each stanza of *How to Tell Wild Animals* ends with a rhyming couplet.

**Reason (R):** *How to Tell Wild Animals* is written in free verse without rhyme.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: each stanza ends cc. R is false: the scheme is ababcc.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The chameleon in *How to Tell Wild Animals* attacks the reader like the other animals.

**Reason (R):** In *How to Tell Wild Animals*, you identify the chameleon by the fact that you cannot see it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: this lizard is tiny and harmless. R is true: seeing nothing is the test.

questions.stem_md: True or false: *How to Tell Wild Animals* is meant to be a serious scientific guide.
questions.solution_md: **False.** It only pretends to be a guide; it is really a humorous poem.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in *How to Tell Wild Animals*, the hyena and the crocodile share one stanza.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Stanza 5 offers a rule for telling them apart.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the unusual spellings in *How to Tell Wild Animals* are printing errors.
questions.solution_md: **False.** They are deliberate: poetic licence for rhyme, rhythm and humour.

questions.stem_md: True or false: each stanza of *How to Tell Wild Animals* ends with a pair of rhyming lines.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The ababcc scheme ends every stanza with a couplet.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the animals in the order in which *How to Tell Wild Animals* describes them.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Lion → tiger → leopard → bear → crocodile and hyena → chameleon.
